name: Polymarket versus Kalshi BTC pair-cost spread
description: Cost of locking a one-dollar payout on each venue alone and across the two venues, for the aligned market pair. It is multi-market scoped on the same two legs and the same exact_close alignment rule as btc.multi.prediction_dislocation@1.0.0. The single-venue legs are consumed verbatim: kalshi_pair_cost and kalshi_fee_adjusted_pair_cost are the published pair_cost and fee_adjusted_pair_cost of btc.kalshi.pair_cost_state@1.0.0, and the polymarket pair likewise from btc.polymarket.pair_cost_state@1.0.0; this identity never re-derives a fee formula. pair_cost_spread is polymarket_fee_adjusted_pair_cost minus kalshi_fee_adjusted_pair_cost and cheaper_venue names the smaller of the two. The two cross legs buy the affirmative outcome on one venue and the negative outcome on the other: cross_pair_cost_up_kalshi is (kalshi affirmative_ask plus the published kalshi yes_leg_fee) plus (polymarket negative_ask plus the published polymarket down_leg_fee) minus one, and cross_pair_cost_up_polymarket is the mirror using polymarket affirmative_ask with its up_leg_fee and kalshi negative_ask with its no_leg_fee. best_cross_pair_cost is the smaller of the two cross legs and best_cross_direction names it, or none when neither leg is computable. state applies the same vocabulary and thresholds as the single-venue identity to best_cross_pair_cost: locked_profit when it is negative, premium when it exceeds premium_threshold, fair otherwise; premium_threshold defaults to 0.01 and is read from the venue identities rather than redeclared. lock_is_conditional is true whenever the two rules cards differ in settlement_benchmark, comparator, tie_outcome or strike, which is the standing case today: a negative cross pair cost is NOT a risk-free lock, because the two contracts can settle inconsistently, and the field says so on every update. Ready output requires both venue pair_cost_state inputs ready, both quotes no more than 10000 milliseconds old, and the leg alignment satisfied. Decimal outputs are rounded to eight places using round-half-to-even.
